new.title: Meeting with Joanne — accessions, numbering, standards, capacity
new.body:
Four questions that are really one conversation. Worth a meeting rather than four emails.

### 1. How do accessions physically arrive
Everything built so far assumes Box is the source. The six Box folders are **extracts copied
from drives, not the drives** — so this is probably not how real accessions come in.

- What physically shows up? Where is the media stored? Who can connect one to a machine?
- How many are queued, and in what condition?
- Does anything warrant forensic imaging rather than a file copy?

If drives get mounted rather than uploaded, the source layer needs a filesystem path, and
"download only what survives triage" stops applying — a mounted drive is already local.

### 2. Accession numbering
Box folders are named `2620267_FemTech`, `2620191_MichaelHart`, `1513059_DonCrummey`,
`2415001_VCResearch`. Those prefixes look like accession numbers already in use.

The schema uses them as `source_id`, and **`file_uid` is derived from it**. Getting this wrong
means a full re-crawl. Confirm the format, who assigns them, and what to use when an accession
has none yet.

### 3. Metadata standard
Dublin Core is the working assumption, IPTC for images. Confirm, or name the institutional
profile or EAD requirement instead. This fixes the `dc_*` columns.

### 4. Review capacity
How many items per week can the Archives team realistically review? Thresholds set without
knowing this produce a queue nobody works through.

### Also
- Where should processed output land in Box, separate from source material?
- A directory listing of one real drive, even before access is sorted — it costs nothing and
  replaces two of our biggest assumptions.

Reference: [W1 schema §1.4](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/W1_manifest_schema_v1.md) · [W3 worksheet](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/worksheets/W3_storage_and_ingest_assessment.md)

new.title: Appraisal policy and a labelled sample
new.body:
Without a written definition of what "important" means, triage cannot be built or measured.

**Why this matters, concretely.** In the image POC, of 79 flagged images: 13 clearly correct,
8 clearly wrong, **58 (73%) ambiguous**. That is not a model failure — it is what happens when
criteria were never written precisely enough for anyone, human or machine, to be consistent.

### The ask, scoped realistically
- [ ] Written appraisal policy — categories always retained, routinely disposable, mandatory review
- [ ] **Start with 50 files, two archivists labelling independently.** If they disagree with
      each other, that is the finding: the criteria need tightening before scaling the exercise.
- [ ] Only then consider the larger 300–500 file set

50 files is cheap to try and tells us whether the bigger ask is worth making.

Reference: [pipeline design §6](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/pipeline-design.md)

new.title: Manifest schema v1 — review and sign off
new.body:
Schema v1 is drafted and decided — 116 columns, stage ownership defined, enforceable code.
I made the calls so we could move; **this is your pass to disagree.**

**Docs:** [W1_manifest_schema_v1.md](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/W1_manifest_schema_v1.md)
**Code:** [manifest.py](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/src/schema/manifest.py) · [validate.py](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/src/schema/validate.py)

### Worth arguing about
- **One row per path, never collapsed.** A file in three places is three archival facts. Dedupe
  is a decision (`duplicate_of`), not a representation.
- **`file_uid` is deterministic** — blake2b of `source_id + path_norm`. Re-crawling yields the
  same keys so generations join. The catch: a wrong `source_id` means a full re-crawl.
- **Per-stage status columns**, null = not reached. `WHERE s03_status IS NULL` is the work queue.
- **Text and embeddings live outside the manifest**, pointers only.
- **`layer` is derived, never authored** — recomputed from decisions so it cannot drift.

- [ ] Read the schema doc
- [ ] Run `validate.py` against the fixture
- [ ] Raise disagreements here
- [ ] Sign the worksheet

Two bugs found while testing, both worth understanding: NaN is truthy in Python, so
`if row.get("duplicate_of")` classified **every** row as layer 0 — triage would have looked
like it was rejecting everything. And adding ~100 columns one at a time fragments the
DataFrame: fine at 5 rows, awful at 5 million.

new.title: Stage 01 — walk, hash, and identify against the schema
new.body:
The filesystem equivalent of the Box inventory, writing through `src/schema/manifest.py`.

- [ ] Walk records path, size, timestamps, depth; full original path preserved verbatim
- [ ] SHA-256 computed locally; Box SHA-1 retained in `content_sha1`
- [ ] Siegfried joined for `s01_puid`, `s01_format_name`, `s01_id_confidence`
- [ ] `s01_ext_mismatch` populated — this measures how wrong POC 2's extension routing was
- [ ] `path_flags` and `date_flags` populated
- [ ] `enforce()` on every write; nothing bypasses the schema
- [ ] 10,000 files in under a minute
- [ ] `validate.report()` passes

**Open question from the schema, item 9:** whole-file SHA-256 is the current decision. Revisit
if an accession turns out to be dominated by multi-gigabyte video, where head+tail+size would be
far faster. The inventory numbers will tell us.

new.title: Stage 02a — free filters, and measure the reduction
new.body:
Zero-cost exclusions: exact duplicates by hash, NSRL known files, zero-byte, `~$` lock files,
`.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, caches, `node_modules`, `.git` internals.

- [ ] Duplicate collapse writes `duplicate_of` and `duplicate_count`; **no rows removed**
- [ ] NSRL RDS obtained and joined
- [ ] Structural exclusions recorded in `s02_structural_exclusion`
- [ ] **Reduction percentage measured and posted here**

That number is the argument for the whole architecture. Get it real rather than assumed — and
remember Box extracts will understate it badly, because they contain no OS files.

new.title: Stage 02b — smart text peek
new.body:
A flat first-2KB is not enough. Documents opening with letterhead, cover pages or a blank
scanned page all look identical in their first 2KB, and on institutional material that is a
large fraction of everything.

~6KB budget, sampled structurally: head after front matter, tail (conclusions and signatures are
often the most identifying part), three strided middle samples, plus headings and TOC entries.

- [ ] Structured peek implemented, writes `s02_peek_text`, `s02_peek_method`, `s02_peek_tier`
- [ ] **Compared against flat first-2KB on the same files** — show the difference
- [ ] Keyword extraction compared against embedding raw text (boilerplate dominates raw peeks)
- [ ] Escalation ladder working — most files resolve at tier 1

Reference: [pipeline design §5](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/pipeline-design.md)

new.title: Stage 02c — scoring and folder-context weighting
new.body:
Score each file, aggregate to folder, propagate back down.

- [ ] Embeddings computed and stored **outside** the manifest, keyed on `file_uid`
- [ ] `s02_file_score` and `s02_folder_score` kept **separate**
- [ ] Folder weighting: a weak file in a coherent folder gets promoted; a strong-looking file in
      a junk folder gets demoted
- [ ] `s02_rationale` is human-readable
- [ ] `layer` computed via `compute_layer()`, never authored by hand

Keeping the two scores separate is the point: "included because its folder is 70% significant"
is an auditable reason; a single blended number is not.

Depends on the appraisal policy for the exemplars.

new.title: Agree human oversight thresholds
new.body:
Proposed starting position — to negotiate, not impose:

| Situation | Oversight |
|---|---|
| Anything flagged sensitive | 100% human review, always |
| Layer 0–1 exclusions, first accession | 100% review — the first one is calibration |
| Layer 0–1, later accessions | Stratified 5–10% plus the borderline band |
| Auto-promoted files | Stratified audit 5–10% |
| Deletion of anything | Explicit human approval, batch level, recorded |

**Establish review capacity first.** Thresholds set without knowing weekly capacity produce a
queue nobody works through.

Reference: [scope doc — governance](https://terbe2022.github.io/RIMS-Archival-Project-/#/x-governance)

new.title: Re-benchmark the serving stack for text
new.body:
POC 1 measured 34.8 sec/row via `subprocess.run()` against the Ollama CLI, which reloads model
weights on every call. That is an implementation artefact, not a model limit.

The image pipeline went 22.2 hrs → 3.7 hrs on the same L4 by migrating to vLLM — 6.22×, of which
3.6× was purely the serving stack. Expect something comparable here.

- [ ] Same workload measured three ways: CLI, Ollama serve, vLLM
- [ ] Results posted here and `docs/pipeline-design.md` updated

Prior work: [image throughput](https://taylererbe.com/archival-image-throughput-evaluation.html)

new.title: Compare three text models on the same 20 documents
new.body:
Same documents, same prompt. Quality and speed recorded here.

**The nuance that matters for metadata:** more detail is not better. A larger model writes more
fluent prose and invents plausible creators and dates more confidently. For Dublin Core fields we
want *extraction*, not *generation* — small model, constrained schema, required to emit `null`
rather than guess.

- [ ] Three models compared
- [ ] Note where each invents rather than extracts on factual fields
- [ ] Recommendation for the enrichment default

Reference: [scope doc — models](https://terbe2022.github.io/RIMS-Archival-Project-/#/x-models)

new.title: Compare three vision models on the same 20 images
new.body:
Same images, same prompt. Include `moondream` as the local baseline and `qwen2.5-vl` as the
likely upgrade from llava-llama3.

**Carry forward from POC 3:** keep description and classification as **separate steps**. LLaVA
produced rationales that correctly described racialised content while returning
`offensive: false` — the description was right and the judgment was wrong. That split is why the
semantic method worked, and why it was ~200× faster.

- [ ] Three models compared on quality and speed
- [ ] Re-run against the same 1,000 images from POC 3 so results are comparable
- [ ] Split-step design confirmed as the default

Reference: [POC 3](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/poc/03-image-classification/) · [taxonomy](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/poc/03-image-classification/data/Sensitive_Content_Taxonomy_DataFrame.csv)

new.title: Decide: adopt ePADD for email, or keep our own lane
new.body:
A genuine build-versus-adopt fork. ePADD is Stanford's email appraisal, redaction and discovery
tool for archives, and it directly overlaps POC 1.

Either it becomes the delivery interface for email and we feed it, or we keep our own lane.
Worth deciding rather than drifting.

- [ ] Ask Brent what RIMS currently uses for email archiving and e-discovery
- [ ] Decision recorded here **with the reasoning**

new.title: Stage 03 — extraction routing table
new.body:
Route on the verified PRONOM PUID from Stage 01, **not** the extension.

- [ ] Routing expressed as **data, not control flow** — a table of format class → lane →
      extractor → cost tier. Adding a format becomes adding a row.
- [ ] Header-only reads for scientific, geospatial and 3D formats — the header *is* the metadata
- [ ] Structural sampling for long documents; skip blank leading pages on scans
- [ ] Encoding detection for legacy plain text (CP1252, Latin-1, UTF-16)
- [ ] Unhandled formats degrade gracefully to technical metadata plus folder context

Reference: [gap analysis](https://github.com/terbe2022/RIMS-Archival-Project-/blob/main/docs/file-type-gap-analysis.md)

new.title: Stage 04 — enrichment lanes
new.body:
Only files that survive triage reach here.

- [ ] **Email:** parse, explode threads, extract headers, mask PII with Presidio, then summarise.
      **Mask before summarising, never after.**
- [ ] **Image:** downsample, extract EXIF/IPTC/XMP, describe, then classify sensitivity as a
      separate auditable step, then OCR if text-bearing
- [ ] **Document:** structural sampling, summary, doc-type inference, PII scan
- [ ] **Tabular:** describe what the dataset *is* — schema, columns, ranges — not what it contains
- [ ] Prompt templates versioned; `s04_model` and `s04_prompt_version` recorded
- [ ] Structured output enforced; model must emit `null` rather than guess

**Known defects to fix, not inherit:** the header regex assumes a fixed field order and returns
`None` on anything else; the thread splitter only matches the English `-----Original Message-----`
delimiter; Presidio tagged a US phone number as `UK_NHS`.

Depends on the PII mapping store decision.

new.title: Stage 05 — metadata and the Dublin Core crosswalk
new.body:
- [ ] Crosswalk from manifest columns to Dublin Core, built as **configuration** so a change in
      target is a mapping change rather than a rewrite
- [ ] IPTC/XMP written back for images via ExifTool
- [ ] Provenance block: source, verbatim original path, hashes, PUID, ingest timestamp,
      pipeline version, model, prompt version
- [ ] `s05_generated_fields` records which DC fields a machine wrote
- [ ] Second-pass triage re-ranks using the generated metadata

**Leave a field blank rather than guessing.** An archivist reading a finding aid should be able
to tell what a machine wrote. Blank beats confidently wrong.

Depends on the metadata standard being confirmed.

new.title: Stage 06 — index, search and delivery
new.body:
POC 2 proved this works and it is what stakeholders responded to most strongly.

- [ ] Vector index over summaries and descriptions
- [ ] **Hybrid retrieval** — semantic plus keyword. Researchers search for exact names and grant
      numbers as often as concepts.
- [ ] Hierarchical browse alongside search
- [ ] Verbatim original path returned on every hit
- [ ] An interface the Archives team can actually use — POC 2 ran through a notebook CLI

new.title: Build the review queue interface
new.body:
The review queue is a first-class output, not a byproduct.

- [ ] Reviewer sees layer 3 by default, can drill into any layer beneath
- [ ] Column subset from `REVIEWER_VIEW` — those must stay human-readable
- [ ] Override writes `rv_*` columns plus an append-only review log
- [ ] Machine decision preserved when overridden

Machine/human disagreement is the most valuable signal we will get — it is how we find out the
appraisal policy is ambiguous.

new.title: Throughput model and drive sizing calculator
new.body:
The Archives needs to prioritise accessions and schedule staff review time. That requires
measurement, not estimation.

- [ ] Per-stage timing instrumented into the manifest
- [ ] Benchmark on a **representative** sample, not a convenient one — format mix drives cost
      more than file count does
- [ ] Sweep batch size, quantisation level, concurrency, persistent server vs per-call
- [ ] Sizing model: file count and format mix in, wall-clock out
- [ ] Recommended processing order across the accession queue

Blocked in practice until a real drive exists — format mix and triage retention are the two
dominant variables and both are currently assumptions.

The calculator on the [scope doc](https://terbe2022.github.io/RIMS-Archival-Project-/#/s07) already reproduces the measured image figures.

The first issue set was written before we knew what was actually in Box, before the manifest
